The proposed framework is evaluated on the BJTU-RAO benchmark,
which reproduces bogie fault conditions using a half-scale laboratory
test rig under controlled operating conditions. Although the dataset
provides diverse fault states and reliable ground-truth labels, it does
not reproduce all sources of variability encountered in real railway
operation. Factors such as long-term component degradation, environ-
mental conditions, sensor aging, and variations in sensor placement
across different rolling-stock configurations are not explicitly repre-
sented. The generalization demonstrated in this study should therefore
be understood in the context of unseen combinations of operating con-
ditions within the benchmark, rather than as evidence of direct transfer
to real-world railway data.

1 INTRODUCTION
The rapid development of high-speed railway systems has significantly
increased the demand for intelligent maintenance solutions capable of
ensuring safe, reliable, and uninterrupted operation. As train speeds
and operational complexity continue to grow, maintaining the health of
critical mechanical subsystems has become a key challenge for railway
operators.
Among these subsystems, the bogie plays a fundamental role in
vehicle stability, traction, and running safety. Within the bogie assem-
bly, axle bearings are particularly susceptible to degradation because
they operate under high rotational speeds, heavy mechanical loads, and
continuously varying working conditions. If left undetected, bearing de-

The proposed framework is evaluated on the BJTU-RAO benchmark,
which reproduces bogie fault conditions using a half-scale laboratory
test rig under controlled operating conditions. Although the dataset
provides diverse fault states and reliable ground-truth labels, it does
not reproduce all sources of variability encountered in real railway

The rapid development of high-speed railway systems has significantly
increased the demand for intelligent maintenance solutions capable of
ensuring safe, reliable, and uninterrupted operation. As train speeds
and operational complexity continue to grow, maintaining the health of
critical mechanical subsystems has become a key challenge for railway
operators.
Among these subsystems, the bogie plays a fundamental role in
vehicle stability, traction, and running safety. Within the bogie assem-
bly, axle bearings are particularly susceptible to degradation because
they operate under high rotational speeds, heavy mechanical loads, and
continuously varying working conditions. If left undetected, bearing de-

dataset, developed by the State Key Laboratory of Advanced Rail
Autonomous Operation at Beijing Jiaotong University. As the first
